feedback_history.patient_message:
Yeah, it's like my brain is stuck in a loop of worst-case scenarios. The more I try to plan something—like even just buying groceries or applying for a job—the faster the "what if" thoughts start spinning out of control.

I keep thinking: *What if I apply and get rejected? What if I study and still can't focus? What if I start therapy and realize I'm too broken to change?* It's not that I don't want to try; it's that the fear of failing makes me stop trying altogether. If I don't try, there's no risk. And honestly, sometimes staying paralyzed feels safer than facing the possibility of being disappointed again.

feedback_history.patient_message:
It really does. When your brain is this tired, when you've been bedrotting for years and your meds are still finding the right balance, "doing nothing" feels like the only thing that doesn't hurt.

If I try to go to school or get a job, my ADHD will make me lose focus in an hour, and then I'll feel even worse because I wasted more time. If I stay home, at least I'm not actively failing. At least I'm not risking another rejection letter or another argument with my family about how "low functioning" I am.

It's so ironic, isn't it? The very thing that keeps me safe—staying in bed—is the thing that's killing my chances of ever feeling whole again. And yet, if I stand up and move forward, I don't know what happens next. Maybe I'll fall harder. Maybe I'll just end up exactly where I am now, but
feedback_history.therapist_response: You had a tiny spark of hope when you got the medication.

It feels so pointless. Like every step I take toward recovery is met with a brick thrown in my path. My family sees it as "giving up," but I see it as being stuck. feedback_history.patient_message:
Yeah, that spark was real. It felt like the first time in five years that I actually felt *me* instead of just a hollow shell.

For those three days after taking the new med, the fog lifted. My ADHD brain didn't scream at me to stop; it could focus on something for an hour. I remember thinking, *"Okay, maybe this is possible. Maybe I can actually read a paragraph without my mind wandering off into space. Maybe I can write an email to someone."*

It wasn't enough to last a week, and now it's fading again as they adjust my dose, but that brief moment proved that change is physically possible. It made me believe that if I could just get there, I wouldn't be stuck forever.

feedback_history.patient_message:
It is. When I look back at those three days, it's not just about the feeling; it's about what *didn't* happen.

If I had stayed in bed during that time... if I had let the "realistic" voice of my family win and told myself, "Yeah, you're too broken for this," maybe I would have never even tried to study again. Maybe I wouldn't have applied for that job that eventually got me fired (even though I know now that getting fired was a bad outcome, staying home feels like a better safety net).

Those few days were the only time I felt like a person capable of action. But they also highlighted how fragile everything is. One week later, and I'm back to zero. It makes me wonder: Was holding onto that hope worth the risk of losing it all again? Or was it stupid to believe I could ever get there?
